The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) has temporarily suspended ongoing training activities at its two training colleges to allow further consultations with the Federal Character Commission (FCC) over concerns surrounding its ongoing recruitment exercise.
The Service disclosed the decision in a statement issued on Friday by its National Public Relations Officer, Abdullahi Maiwada.
It said the decision followed engagements between the commission and a delegation of the NCS, during which both parties reaffirmed their commitment to resolving the issues through constructive dialogue, mutual understanding and continued institutional collaboration.
The Comptroller-General of Customs (CGC), Bashir Adeniyi, reaffirmed the NCS’s commitment to constructive engagement with relevant government institutions in the national interest.
Mr Adeniyi also acknowledged the FCC’s role in promoting national unity, fairness and equitable representation in public service appointments.
The CGC acknowledged the FCC’s critical role in promoting national unity, fairness and equitable representation in public service appointments, noting the importance of its constitutional mandate in strengthening inclusiveness and ensuring that federal character principles are upheld across the Federation.
“The NCS values its longstanding relationship with the FCC and remains confident that the ongoing dialogue will provide an opportunity to address the concerns raised in a mutually beneficial manner, while reinforcing the shared commitment of both institutions to fairness, national cohesion and effective public service delivery,” the statement read.

The Service said it remains committed to upholding the highest standards of institutional accountability and transparency in the discharge of its responsibilities.
NCS added that it will continue to engage constructively with relevant government institutions, strengthen inter-agency relationships and pursue resolutions that promote public confidence, national cohesion and the effective delivery of its mandate.
The dispute stems from the NCS’s 2025 recruitment exercise, which began with an advertisement for 3,927 vacancies that later attracted more than 573,000 applications.
The Service published its final list of 3,852 successful candidates in July 2026, and training began on 9 October at the Nigeria Customs Command and Staff College, Gwagwalada, Abuja.
However, some applicants alleged that they had been excluded from training despite completing the required screening and documentation exercises and seeing their names on the published lists.
On 19 October the NCS said 397 applicants were screened out over issues relating to substance abuse, age, physical fitness, and documentation, clarifying that inclusion in the final shortlist does not automatically guarantee enlistment into the Service.
FCC subsequently raised concerns over the process, citing complaints from more than 500 applicants, and called for the suspension of training on 22 October pending an investigation into compliance with federal character principles.
The commission later sued the NCS and its Comptroller-General, Mr Adeniyi, on 13 November, accusing them of failing to provide information on the recruitment exercise.
